title: Type Conversion and Casting
description: Widening and narrowing numeric conversions, explicit casting, and reference-type casting.
objectives: Understand widening (implicit) vs. narrowing (explicit) numeric conversion
Perform explicit casts and understand when data can be lost

content.heading: Widening and Narrowing Numeric Conversion
content.body:
Widening conversion moves a value to a type that can represent a strictly larger range (e.g., int to long, or int to double) and happens implicitly/automatically, since no information can be lost. Narrowing conversion moves a value to a type with a smaller range (e.g., double to int, or int to byte) and requires an explicit cast, because it can lose information: double d = 9.75; int i = (int) d; truncates to 9 (not rounds), and casting an int outside a smaller type's range wraps around unpredictably.

Mixed-type arithmetic follows widening rules automatically: int / int performs integer division (discarding the remainder), but if either operand is a double, the whole expression is promoted to double before dividing.

content.heading: Explicit Casting and Reference Casting
content.body: The cast syntax is (targetType) expression: (int) 9.75, (double) someInt. For reference types, casting works differently: it doesn't convert data, it reinterprets a reference as a more specific (or less specific) type in a class hierarchy. Upcasting (treating a subclass reference as its superclass type, e.g., Object o = new Dog()) is always safe and implicit. Downcasting (treating a superclass reference as a more specific subclass, e.g., Dog d = (Dog) o) requires an explicit cast and is only safe if the object's actual runtime type really is that subclass (or a further subclass of it) — otherwise it throws a ClassCastException at runtime. The instanceof operator lets you check an object's actual type before attempting a downcast.

content.explanation: (int) price truncates rather than rounds. The instanceof check before the downcast avoids a potential ClassCastException if obj had actually held a different type at runtime.

keyPoints: Widening (small type -> large type) happens implicitly; narrowing requires an explicit cast
Casting a double to int truncates the decimal part — it does not round
Upcasting (subclass reference -> superclass type) is implicit and always safe
Downcasting requires an explicit cast and can throw ClassCastException if the actual object isn't that subclass
commonMistakes: Expecting (int) someDouble to round instead of truncate
Performing int / int and being surprised by integer division instead of a decimal result
Downcasting without an instanceof check first, risking a runtime ClassCastException
